title: Putting a Gene in the Wrong Place
endLine: Misexpression tests what a factor can impose, not what tissue needs.

scenes.tts: One protein marks a stripe of cells. Does it command their fate? Watching where it appears in an embryo cannot separate cause from label. To test its power, put that protein into cells that normally lack it.
scenes.caption: One protein marks a stripe of cells. Does it command their fate? Watching where it appears in an embryo cannot separate cause from label. To test its power, put that protein into cells that normally lack it.
scenes.visual: Schematic cross-section of an embryonic neural tube fills most of the frame height, with a bright glowing stripe on its wall that gently shimmers. A bold question mark rises beside the stripe as the narrator asks if it commands fate. Two short tags, 'Cause?' and 'Label?', briefly branch and fade, then a glowing dot lifts out of the stripe and arcs into a dark zone of cells that lack it (schematic, no molecular structures).
scenes.narration: One protein marks a stripe of cells. Does it command their fate? Watching where it appears in an embryo cannot separate cause from label. To test its power, put that protein into cells that normally lack it.

scenes.visual: The schematic neural tube dims softly in the background while the title 'Putting a Gene in the Wrong Place' settles at center in large high-contrast text; slow ambient glow drifts along the tube wall.

scenes.tts: Making a protein in cells that normally lack it is called misexpression, or ectopic expression. To test a gene in a chick neural tube, researchers inject its DNA inside. At first, that DNA floats in the hollow center, outside the cells.
scenes.caption: Making a protein in cells that normally lack it is called misexpression, or ectopic expression. To test a gene in a chick neural tube, researchers inject its DNA inside. At first, that DNA floats in the hollow center, outside the cells.
scenes.visual: Return to the same full-height schematic chick neural tube cross-section, with left and right walls framing a hollow central canal. Label 'Misexpression' appears briefly as a dark zone lights up. A fine schematic micropipette enters the hollow center from above and releases drifting glowing DNA dots (schematic, no molecular structures) that swirl freely inside the canal without crossing into either cell wall.
scenes.narration: Making a protein in cells that normally lack it is called misexpression, or ectopic expression. To test a gene in a chick neural tube, researchers inject its DNA inside. At first, that DNA floats in the hollow center, outside the cells.

scenes.tts: Next, brief electric pulses push DNA into cells on one side of the tube. That is electroporation. Only the pulsed side makes the protein; the opposite side stays an untouched control. Adding a factor elsewhere tests sufficiency: what it can impose, not what tissue needs.
scenes.caption: Next, brief electric pulses push DNA into cells on one side of the tube. That is electroporation. Only the pulsed side makes the protein; the opposite side stays an untouched control. Adding a factor elsewhere tests sufficiency: what it can impose, not what tissue needs.
scenes.visual: In the same schematic neural tube, brief glowing electric pulse arcs sweep left to right across the canal. The drifting schematic DNA dots surge exclusively into the right wall's cells, which brighten in a new colour while the left wall stays unchanged, labelled 'Control side' on the left and 'Electroporated side' on the right. Below the tube, a clean banner settles: 'Tests sufficiency: what it can impose'.
scenes.narration: Next, brief electric pulses push DNA into cells on one side of the tube. That is electroporation. Only the pulsed side makes the protein; the opposite side stays an untouched control. Adding a factor elsewhere tests sufficiency: what it can impose, not what tissue needs.

scenes.tts: Predict a result here. Just above the floor plate, stripe p three makes N K X two point two. The stripe above, p M N, carries a low level of Pax six. Each factor switches the other off at their border. Now pulse it into p M N on the right. What happens to Pax six and the border?
scenes.caption: Predict a result here. Just above the floor plate, stripe p3 makes Nkx2.2. The stripe above, pMN, carries a low level of Pax6. Each factor switches the other off at their border. Now pulse it into pMN on the right. What happens to Pax6 and the border?
scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly onto the lower half of the same schematic neural tube cross-section. The bottom strip lights up first, labelled 'Floor plate'. Directly above it on both sides, a coloured band labelled 'p3: Nkx2.2' meets an upper band labelled 'pMN: Pax6' at a crisp horizontal border line, with schematic double-blunt inhibition arrows pushing against each other across the line. Brief electric pulse arcs then drive schematic Nkx2.2 dots into the right pMN band as the question appears above: 'What happens to Pax6 and the border?'.
scenes.narration: Predict a result here. Just above the floor plate, stripe p3 makes Nkx2.2. The stripe above, pMN, carries a low level of Pax6. Each factor switches the other off at their border. Now pulse it into pMN on the right. What happens to Pax6 and the border?

scenes.visual: Hold the schematic neural tube with the question 'What happens to Pax6 and the border?' still visible at top; the right pMN cells gently shimmer with incoming schematic Nkx2.2 dots while the viewer thinks.

scenes.tts: On the pulsed right side, N K X two point two switches Pax six off. The border shifts upward into what was p M N. Meanwhile, the untouched left side holds its normal border in the same embryo. Briscoe and colleagues used chick electroporation like this to map opposing borders.
scenes.caption: On the pulsed right side, Nkx2.2 switches Pax6 off. The border shifts upward into what was pMN. Meanwhile, the untouched left side holds its normal border in the same embryo. Briscoe and colleagues used chick electroporation like this to map opposing borders.
scenes.visual: In the same schematic neural tube, the right pMN cells lose their Pax6 colour and turn into the p3 colour, visibly pushing the horizontal border line upward on the right side only. A dashed reference line extends across from the untouched left border to make the upward shift unmistakable, with a short tag 'Same-embryo control' on the left.
scenes.narration: On the pulsed right side, Nkx2.2 switches Pax6 off. The border shifts upward into what was pMN. Meanwhile, the untouched left side holds its normal border in the same embryo. Briscoe and colleagues used chick electroporation like this to map opposing borders.

scenes.tts: Still, misexpression can mislead. A factor is sufficient only in the cells and stage tested, using their existing machinery. Shifting a border in one tissue cannot prove a gene builds an organizer anywhere. Nor does it prove the embryo normally needs that gene.
scenes.caption: Still, misexpression can mislead. A factor is sufficient only in the cells and stage tested, using their existing machinery. Shifting a border in one tissue cannot prove a gene builds an organizer anywhere. Nor does it prove the embryo normally needs that gene.
scenes.visual: Pull back slightly on the schematic neural tube. Inside a right-side cell, faint schematic helper shapes already waiting inside the cell light up alongside the added factor, labelled 'Existing cell machinery'. Then a schematic copy of the factor moves to a distant grey tissue patch labelled 'Other tissue', where nothing changes, and a subtle caution icon marks 'Can impose != normal need'.
scenes.narration: Still, misexpression can mislead. A factor is sufficient only in the cells and stage tested, using their existing machinery. Shifting a border in one tissue cannot prove a gene builds an organizer anywhere. Nor does it prove the embryo normally needs that gene.

scenes.tts: Paired controls guard against both traps. To test necessity, researchers pair gain with loss: they delete the gene or block its receptor. To verify the pathway, they repeat delivery in tissue lacking the receptor. If nothing happens there, the effect runs through that pathway.
scenes.caption: Paired controls guard against both traps. To test necessity, researchers pair gain with loss: they delete the gene or block its receptor. To verify the pathway, they repeat delivery in tissue lacking the receptor. If nothing happens there, the effect runs through that pathway.
scenes.visual: Transform the schematic neural tube into two side-by-side schematic comparisons. Left: '+ Gain' adds the factor while '- Loss' deletes the gene or snaps a schematic cap onto a surface receptor notch, checking what fails to form. Right: the same added signal drifts across schematic cells whose receptor notches are removed; the cells stay completely dark, labelled 'No receptor, no effect'.
scenes.narration: Paired controls guard against both traps. To test necessity, researchers pair gain with loss: they delete the gene or block its receptor. To verify the pathway, they repeat delivery in tissue lacking the receptor. If nothing happens there, the effect runs through that pathway.

scenes.tts: With those controls, misexpression unlocked how embryos pattern brains. In 1993, Yann Echelard, Andrew McMahon and colleagues forced Sonic hedgehog on in mice. Where the central nervous system lacked it, floor-plate genes switched on. In 2001, Sato, Araki and Nakamura misexpressed F G F eight b in chick embryos. That signal could turn midbrain roof into cerebellum.
scenes.caption: With those controls, misexpression unlocked how embryos pattern brains. In 1993, Yann Echelard, Andrew McMahon and colleagues forced Sonic hedgehog on in mice. Where the central nervous system lacked it, floor-plate genes switched on. In 2001, Sato, Araki and Nakamura misexpressed FGF8b in chick embryos. That signal could turn midbrain roof into cerebellum.
scenes.visual: Return to the schematic neural tube cross-section: a bright glowing dot labelled 'Shh' is placed in a dark upper wall region and turns those cells into the glowing floor-plate colour, tagged '1993: floor-plate genes'. Then the cross-section morphs smoothly into a schematic side view of a developing chick brain tube: a glowing patch labelled 'FGF8b' on the midbrain roof reshapes that roof into a small schematic folded cerebellum, tagged '2001: midbrain to cerebellum'.
scenes.narration: With those controls, misexpression unlocked how embryos pattern brains. In 1993, Yann Echelard, Andrew McMahon and colleagues forced Sonic hedgehog on in mice. Where the central nervous system lacked it, floor-plate genes switched on. In 2001, Sato, Araki and Nakamura misexpressed FGF8b in chick embryos. That signal could turn midbrain roof into cerebellum.

scenes.tts: In 2002, Anjen Chenn and Christopher Walsh expressed stabilized beta-catenin in mouse neural progenitors. Stabilized means the cell does not break it down. More of those cells kept dividing, enlarging and folding the normally smooth cortex. That showed extra divisions can enlarge the cortex, not how primate cortex grows. Adding shows what a factor can command; deleting shows what tissue requires.

scenes.visual: The schematic side view morphs into a schematic cross-section of a smooth mouse cortex sitting over a row of dividing progenitor cells. Glowing schematic 'β-catenin' keeps those progenitors splitting repeatedly; the cortical sheet expands and buckles into deep schematic folds, tagged '2002: enlarged, folded cortex' alongside a crisp hedge tag 'Not how primates grow'. At the end, the folds settle into two clean icons: '+ Add: command' and '- Delete: require'.
scenes.narration: In 2002, Anjen Chenn and Christopher Walsh expressed stabilized β-catenin in mouse neural progenitors. Stabilized means the cell does not break it down.
